title: India's Tax Authority Makes Foreign Account Data Visible to Taxpayers
excerpt: A new CBDT order uploads overseas bank accounts, investments, and income data from over 100 countries into taxpayers' Annual Information Statements, giving the taxman — and you — full visibility.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • CBDT's July 8 order mandates foreign financial data from 100+ countries in taxpayers' Annual Information Statements.
  • Data for 2022, 2023, and 2024 is available; 2025 data expected by late 2026.
  • ROR taxpayers must report all foreign assets; penalties for non-disclosure can reach Rs 10 lakh annually.
  • NRIs have no new disclosure obligations; returned NRIs face immediate compliance once classified as ROR.
  • Taxpayers can access foreign asset data via the e-Filing portal's Compliance Portal.

India's Central Board of Direct Taxes has pulled back the curtain on overseas financial data. A CBDT order dated July 8, 2026, directs that foreign account information received from more than 100 partner countries be uploaded directly into individual taxpayers' Annual Information Statements on the Income Tax e-Filing portal.

Until now, data exchanged under the OECD's Common Reporting Standard (CRS) and the US-India Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA) agreement sat with the income tax department internally. Taxpayers had no way to see what the department already knew about their foreign holdings. That asymmetry is now over.

What Shows Up in Your AIS

The uploaded data covers foreign bank accounts, custodial accounts, financial investments, interest income, dividend income, and other foreign-source financial income. For the growing number of Indian residents who hold US stocks through investment apps, receive RSUs or ESOPs from multinational employers, or maintain overseas bank accounts from prior NRI stints, the change is immediate and personal.

Data for calendar years 2022, 2023, and 2024 is currently available in the AIS. The CBDT has a 90-day window to upload new data once received from partner jurisdictions, and information for calendar year 2025 is expected to appear by September–October 2026, according to the CBDT note.

"The department's secret file on your foreign income will now be visible on your own screen."

— CAClubIndia tax analysis

Who Needs to Act — and Who Doesn't

The compliance burden depends entirely on residency status. Non-Resident Indians have no new disclosure obligations from this order. Their foreign income is not taxable in India, and the AIS entries are informational only.

The real pressure falls on Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR) taxpayers. They must report every foreign asset — bank accounts, shares, ESOPs, mutual funds — in Schedule FA of their income tax return, regardless of whether the asset generates income. Even a dormant UK bank account with £200 sitting idle must be disclosed.

Returned NRIs in their RNOR (Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident) transition window have some relief, as their disclosure rules remain relaxed. But the moment they become full ROR, all foreign accounts — including ones from years ago — must be declared.

Penalties and Compliance Stakes

Who Needs to Disclose?
Resident and Ordinarily Resident (ROR)
Must report all foreign assets
Non-Resident Indians (NRIs)
No new disclosure obligations
Returned NRIs (Transitioning to ROR)
Immediate compliance required

The stakes are steep. Under the Black Money (Undisclosed Foreign Income and Assets) and Imposition of Tax Act, failure to disclose foreign assets by an ROR taxpayer can attract penalties of Rs 10 lakh per year. Some relief is available if total foreign assets remain below Rs 20 lakh, but the disclosure requirement applies regardless of the value.

The CBDT has stressed that the AIS data is "facilitative in nature" and not a complete record of a taxpayer's foreign assets. Taxpayers remain responsible for fully disclosing all foreign assets and income in Schedule FA and Schedule FSI of their returns, whether or not the information appears in AIS.

Critically, taxpayers with foreign assets cannot file ITR-1 or ITR-4. They must use ITR-2 or ITR-3, which include the necessary schedules for foreign asset reporting.

What NRIs and Returned Indians Should Do Now

The Income Tax Department has begun sending SMS and email alerts to taxpayers about the new facility. To access the data, taxpayers can log into the e-Filing portal, navigate to AIS, open the Compliance Portal, select Reports, then Foreign Assets Information, and download a PDF for the relevant calendar year.

Navigating Compliance and Penalties
›Penalties for ROR non-disclosure can reach Rs 10 lakh annually.
›Taxpayers must use ITR-2 or ITR-3 for foreign asset reporting.
›AIS data is not a complete record; full disclosure is still required.
›Taxpayers can claim Foreign Tax Credit under Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement.

For those who missed disclosing foreign accounts in previous years, the department recommends filing an Updated Return (ITR-U) voluntarily before a notice arrives. Since the department now has data going back to 2022, past omissions are likely to surface during automated matching.

Tax professionals advise reconciling AIS data carefully with ITR filings, particularly because foreign countries report on a calendar year (January–December) basis while Indian returns follow the financial year (April–March). The same income could appear to be unreported if the period mismatch is not accounted for. Taxpayers who have paid tax abroad on the same income can claim a Foreign Tax Credit under the applicable Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement by filing Form 67 before submitting their ITR.
